title: When Can a Cavity Move a Mott Transition? A Spectral-Density Criterion within Gutzwiller Theory
abstract: Can vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations shift a bulk Mott transition? Within the Gutzwiller variational method, we derive a criterion that separates collective spectroscopic hybridization from thermodynamic phase control. We show that a Mott transition shifts only when the electromagnetic environment supplies finite thermodynamic spectral weight with bond-scale variation. A joint frequency--spatial Pauli--Fierz density gives the leading shift. Surface phonon polaritons yield a $d^{-3}$-to-$d^{-5}$ crossover, while finite-coordination variational Monte Carlo supports the predicted critical coefficient and $M/N$ scaling.
summary: The paper develops a criterion within Gutzwiller theory to determine when vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations can shift a Mott insulator transition. The key finding is that this requires the environment to provide finite, spatially varying spectral weight across the electronic hopping bonds. This bridges concepts from quantum optics and strongly correlated materials physics.
main_problem: The study determines the precise criterion by which vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations, such as those from a cavity or surface plasmons, can induce a shift in a bulk Mott metal-insulator transition.
main_result: A Mott transition shifts only if the coupling environment supplies finite thermodynamic spectral weight that varies spatially across the electronic hopping bonds. The magnitude of this shift depends on the joint frequency-spatial Pauli-Fierz density.
method: The analysis employs the Gutzwiller variational method, deriving a critical criterion using the joint frequency–spatial Pauli–Fierz density ($J_{PF}$). This is complemented by Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) simulations for finite coordination systems.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a half-filled Hubbard model coupled to normalized electromagnetic modes or planar phonon-polariton surfaces. The Hamiltonian includes hopping, on-site repulsion ($U$), and the coupling term derived from the cavity environment.
key_observables: Mott boundary shift ($\Delta U_c$); Joint frequency–spatial Pauli–Fierz density ($J_{PF}$); Critical coefficient for phase boundary shift.
important_parameters: Bond-scale variation of spectral weight; Distance scaling ($d^{-3}$ to $d^{-5}$ crossover); Thermodynamic weight ($\eta_\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on Gutzwiller variational approximations, often assuming infinite coordination or using first-order expansions in mode density.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cavity-induced displacement of the Brinkman–Rice boundary and show that only the bond-projected component of the local near-field weight drives the Mott transition shift, causing a crossover in scaling behavior.
paper_structure: The paper develops the criterion by analyzing the coupling Hamiltonian using Gutzwiller theory. It derives the leading shift formula based on $J_{PF}$, applies this to specific environments (like surface polaritons), and validates the results using VMC simulations for finite lattices.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, quantitative link between quantum electrodynamics (vacuum fluctuations) and strongly correlated electron physics. It establishes that simple local density of states is insufficient; the spatial structure of the field coupling to electronic bonds dictates the phase transition outcome.

Solutions of Eq. 6 for νm = r = 1 show that the same gauge-complete coupling lowers Uc through a residual self- polarization penalty for slow modes and bandwidth narrowing for fast modes. Here UBR = 8A0 is the Brinkman–Rice critical interaction in the absence of light–matter coupling.

FIG. 2. Bond-scale field variation controls the surface-polariton shift. (a) Geometry and surface response of 4H-SiC. (b) Cavity-induced shift of the Mott boundary and total local Pauli–Fierz weight versus layer–surface distance. Although the local near-field weight grows as d decreases, only its bond-projected component shifts Uc, producing a crossover from d−3 to d−5. Parameters are given in the panel.

FIG. 3. Finite-coordination validation of the spectral-density criterion. (a) Weak-coupling cavity energy density versus measured double occupancy; its D →0 slope determines the shift of the Mott boundary. (b) The VMC coefficient on N = 24 random regular graphs agrees with the infinite-coordination prediction within 5–7%; error bars include graph-to-graph fluctuations. (c) Separate variation of M and N confirms δe ∝M/N and the vanishing 1/N contribution of a single normalized mode.
